lead: Real gases do not obey μ = μ° + RT ln P, because their molecules attract and repel each other. Fugacity f is the corrected pressure that keeps the logarithmic form exactly true, and φ = f/P, the fugacity coefficient, measures how far the gas is from ideal. Every K-value and every VLE calculation in a simulator rests on fugacity.
prereq: You need chemical potential from chemical potential and phase equilibrium, the compressibility factor and the virial equation of state, and residual properties.

blocks.text: For an ideal gas at fixed temperature, the chemical potential rises logarithmically with pressure: μ = μ°(T) + RT ln(P/P°). Doubling the pressure adds RT ln 2, about 1.7 kJ/mol at 300 K. The derivation assumes molecules do not interact and V = RT/P exactly.

A real gas breaks that assumption. Attraction pulls molecules together, so at moderate pressure the volume is smaller than RT/P, and the simple logarithm no longer gives the correct μ. G. N. Lewis (1901) kept the shape of the equation and replaced pressure by a corrected pressure, the fugacity.

blocks.where: μᵢ is the chemical potential of species i in J/mol; μᵢ° is its value in the reference state at the same T; R = 8.314 J/(mol·K); fᵢ is the fugacity in bar or Pa; fᵢ° is the fugacity of the reference state.

blocks.text: The definition is completed by a limit: fᵢ → Pᵢ (the partial pressure) as P → 0, where every gas becomes ideal. With the usual reference, the pure ideal gas at P° = 1 bar, f° = 1 bar, so fᵢ carries units of pressure.

blocks.where: φᵢ is the fugacity coefficient, dimensionless; Pᵢ is the partial pressure, yᵢP for a gas mixture or P for a pure gas. Some books write the fugacity coefficient as f/P instead of φ.

blocks.text: φ → 1 as P → 0, and an ideal gas has φ = 1 at every pressure, so any value away from 1 measures non-ideality. Because a species has the same μ in every phase at equilibrium, it also has the same fugacity there: equality of fugacities, not of pressures, is the working condition for every VLE calculation.
At fixed temperature dG = V dP for any fluid and dGⁱᵍ = (RT/P) dP for an ideal gas. Integrating the difference from zero pressure gives the residual Gibbs energy, Gᴿ = RT ln φ for a pure fluid.

blocks.where: V is molar volume in m³/mol; R = 8.314 J/(mol·K); T in K; P in Pa; Z = PV/RT is the compressibility factor at the same T and P.

blocks.text: Read the sign. If Z < 1 the gas is more compressible than ideal, f is smaller than P and φ < 1. If Z > 1, φ > 1. As P → 0, Z − 1 shrinks in proportion to P (Z − 1 ≈ BP/RT), so (Z − 1)/P tends to the finite value B/RT. The integrand stays finite, which is why the lower limit can be zero even though P appears in the denominator.

Two routes give the integral quickly. For moderate pressures use the truncated virial equation Z = 1 + BP/RT, which gives ln φ = BP/RT with B in m³/mol. For high pressures, use a cubic equation of state and integrate its Z analytically.

sections.h3: Mixtures, residual Gibbs energy and generalized correlation

blocks.text: In a mixture each species has its own fugacity f̂ᵢ, defined by the same equation μᵢ = μᵢ° + RT ln(f̂ᵢ/fᵢ°), and its own coefficient φ̂ᵢ = f̂ᵢ/(yᵢP), with yᵢ the gas mole fraction. Using the partial molar volume V̄ᵢ, ln φ̂ᵢ = (1/RT) ∫₀ᴾ (V̄ᵢ − RT/P) dP.

blocks.where: Gᴿ is the residual Gibbs energy of the mixture in J/mol; xᵢ is the mole fraction; φ̂ᵢ is the fugacity coefficient of species i in the mixture. For a pure fluid this reduces to ln φ = Gᴿ/RT.

blocks.text: An ideal solution obeys the Lewis-Randall rule f̂ᵢ = xᵢ fᵢpure, so φ̂ᵢ equals the pure-fluid φᵢ at the same T and P (see Chapter 5.5). Real mixtures deviate, and that deviation is what activity coefficients in Chapter 5.7 correct for.

Generalized correlation. Put the Pitzer virial form into the integral: B⁰ = 0.083 − 0.422/Tᵣ<sup>1.6</sup>, B¹ = 0.139 − 0.172/Tᵣ<sup>4.2</sup> and BPc/RTc = B⁰ + ωB¹, with Tᵣ = T/Tc, Pᵣ = P/Pc and ω the acentric factor. The result is ln φ = (Pᵣ/Tᵣ)(B⁰ + ωB¹). It needs only Tc, Pc and ω and holds where the two-term virial equation holds: non-polar or slightly polar gases at low reduced pressure (well below Pᵣ = 1); at higher Pᵣ use a cubic equation of state.

Liquids have a fugacity too. From the saturated liquid, where f = φ<sup>sat</sup>P<sup>sat</sup>, compress the liquid at fixed T (d ln f = V dP/RT): f<sup>l</sup> = φ<sup>sat</sup>P<sup>sat</sup> exp[V<sup>l</sup>(P − P<sup>sat</sup>)/RT], where the exponential is the Poynting factor. For water at 100 °C (P<sup>sat</sup> = 1.013 bar, V<sup>l</sup> = 18.8 cm³/mol, φ<sup>sat</sup> taken as 0.99) at 50 bar the factor is exp(0.0297) = 1.030, so f<sup>l</sup> = 1.03 bar: close to the vapour pressure, not to the system pressure.

spec.aria: Fugacity against pressure from 0 to 10 bar: a dashed diagonal for the ideal gas and a solid curve for the real gas that leaves the diagonal at 1 bar and ends at 7.94 bar when the pressure is 10 bar.

examples.question: A pure gas at 10.0 bar has Z = 0.90, constant from 1.0 bar to 10.0 bar. Below 1.0 bar the gas is ideal. Taking the ideal-gas reference at 1.0 bar, estimate φ and f at 10.0 bar.
steps: Write the working formula: ln φ = ∫₀ᴾ (Z − 1) dP/P. Below 1 bar, Z = 1, so the integrand is zero and that part adds nothing.
Substitute Z = 0.90 for the range 1.0 to 10.0 bar: ln φ = (0.90 − 1) ∫₁<sup>10</sup> dP/P = (−0.10) ln(10.0/1.0).
Exponentiate: φ = e<sup>−0.2303</sup> = 0.7943. The value is below 1, as expected for Z < 1.
Convert to fugacity: f = φP = 0.7943 × 10.0 bar = 7.94 bar.
examples.answer: At 10.0 bar, φ = 0.794 and f = 7.94 bar, lower than the true pressure.
examples.check:
import math
Z = 0.90
P1 = 1.0
P2 = 10.0
lnphi = (Z - 1.0) * math.log(P2 / P1)
phi = math.exp(lnphi)
f = phi * P2
print(round(lnphi, 4))
print(round(phi, 4))
print(round(f, 3))

examples.question: Estimate the fugacity coefficient and fugacity of n-butane at 500 K and 15 bar from the generalized virial (Pitzer) correlation. For n-butane Tc = 425.1 K, Pc = 37.96 bar and ω = 0.200.
steps: Tᵣ = 500/425.1 = 1.1762; Pᵣ = 15/37.96 = 0.3952. Low Pᵣ and Tᵣ above 1: the virial correlation applies.
Check with B itself: B = (B⁰ + ωB¹)RTc/Pc = −2.16 × 10⁻⁴ m³/mol, and BP/RT = −2.16 × 10⁻⁴ × 15 × 10⁵/(8.314 × 500) = −0.0780, the same ln φ.
examples.answer: φ = 0.925 and f = 13.9 bar: n-butane at 500 K and 15 bar escapes as if its pressure were 1.1 bar lower than it is.

traps: Setting f = P for a real gas. That is true only in the ideal-gas limit; using it at 10 bar here would overstate the fugacity by 26 percent.
Mixing reference states: keep the same f° in every step, or the RT ln term picks up a false offset.
Using log₁₀ instead of ln in ln φ = ∫(Z − 1) dP/P. The formula needs natural logarithms throughout.
Taking a liquid's fugacity as the system pressure. It is close to P<sup>sat</sup>: f ≈ φ<sup>sat</sup>P<sup>sat</sup> times the Poynting factor.
Treating φ̂ᵢ of a mixture as the pure φᵢ at the same T and P without checking the Lewis-Randall assumption.

quiz.q: Define fugacity and fugacity coefficient for a pure gas.
quiz.a: Fugacity f is the corrected pressure defined by μ = μ° + RT ln(f/f°), with f → P as P → 0. The fugacity coefficient is φ = f/P, dimensionless, and φ → 1 as P → 0.

quiz.q: Why can μ = μ°(T) + RT ln P not be used for a real gas?
quiz.a: That form comes from dG = V dP with V = RT/P. A real gas has V ≠ RT/P because of intermolecular forces, so it fails; fugacity keeps the same form exact by carrying the correction inside f.

quiz.q: A gas has Z = 0.85 over a range of pressure. Is its fugacity larger or smaller than its pressure, and why?
quiz.a: Z < 1 makes (Z − 1)/P negative, so ln φ is negative, φ < 1 and f < P. The molecules attract each other, the gas escapes less strongly than an ideal gas would, so its effective pressure is lower than the true one.

quiz.q: A gas has Z = 0.95, constant from 1 bar to 8 bar, and is ideal below 1 bar. Find φ and f at 8 bar.
For a pure gas at 300 K and 10 bar, φ = 0.794. Find its residual Gibbs energy.
quiz.a: Gᴿ = RT ln φ = 8.314 × 300 × ln(0.794) = 2494.2 × (−0.2307) = −575 J/mol. The negative sign means the real gas has lower Gibbs energy than the ideal gas at the same T and P.

quiz.q: A binary gas mixture at 300 K has equal mole fractions with ln φ̂₁ = −0.10 and ln φ̂₂ = −0.30. Find Gᴿ of the mixture and say whether the mixture is ideal.
quiz.a: Gᴿ/RT = Σ xᵢ ln φ̂ᵢ = 0.5(−0.10) + 0.5(−0.30) = −0.20, so Gᴿ = −0.20 × 8.314 × 300 = −499 J/mol. Gᴿ ≠ 0, so the mixture is not an ideal gas. Whether it is an ideal solution needs φ̂ᵢ compared with the pure-gas φᵢ at the same T and P, which these data do not give.

beyond: Not for the exam. Simulators such as Aspen Plus and DWSIM compute φ̂ᵢ from an equation of state on every stage of a column; the K-value is the ratio of liquid to vapour fugacity coefficients. Supercritical CO₂ extraction is designed from fugacity coefficients near the critical point. Search next: Peng-Robinson fugacity coefficient, Poynting correction, fugacity of a solid.
